tagline.text: The Philippines' largest lake, with lakeside towns and Talim Island, southeast of Manila

location.label: Location
location.text: A lake southeast of Metro Manila, between Laguna and Rizal provinces

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~2,000 (per person, transport, meals and boat fares)

children.text: Laguna de Bay is the largest lake in the Philippines, with lakeside towns close to central Manila, Talim Island and lovely sunsets. It is not a lake for swimming, but one for taking a boat, visiting villages and watching the evening glow, so go with that in mind.

Laguna de Bay is the largest lake in the Philippines and is known as the third-largest inland body of water in Southeast Asia, after Tonle Sap and Lake Toba. It lies southeast of Metro Manila: Laguna province wraps the west, east and southwest, Rizal province wraps the north to northeast, and the northwestern end touches Metro Manila. The name means "lagoon of Bay," after the town of Bay, and the province of Laguna took its name from the lake. According to Wikipedia, the surface area is about
911km²
, the maximum length east to west is about
47km
, and the maximum width north to south is about
40km
The lake is shaped like a crow's foot, with Talim Island floating in the middle. The average depth is only about
, and even the deepest point, near Diablo Pass, is about

. The lake sits almost at sea level, and its water drains to Manila Bay through the Pasig River, with the Napindan Channel as the outlet. The lake is so wide and shallow because water collected in the Laguna Caldera, a volcanic depression formed by eruptions about 1 million years ago and again 27,000–29,000 years ago. As a result, traces of volcanic terrain can be seen around the shore and across Talim Island.

About 21 major rivers flow into the lake. The river system that runs down from Pagsanjan Falls is said to supply about 35 percent of the inflow, and the Santa Cruz River about 15 percent (the 35 percent figure is consistent across several sources; the 15 percent figure comes from a single Wikipedia-derived source). Water from the Marikina River enters through the Manggahan Floodway. The lake has long been a waterway. The name "Puliran Kasumuran" appears in the Laguna Copperplate Inscription (about AD 900), passenger boats plied it in the Spanish era, and it is still used for freight, irrigation and fish farming. Dozens of cities and towns ring the lake, including Biñan, Cabuyao, Calamba, San Pedro and Santa Rosa in Laguna, Los Baños, Paete and Pila, and Angono, Binangonan, Cardona, Morong, Tanay and Jala-jala in Rizal.

To be honest, Laguna de Bay is not a "postcard beach resort." There is almost no sandy shore, the water is murky, and it is not suited to swimming. Instead, it is a place to drive along lakeside towns near Manila, see fish markets, fish pens and the evening glow, and fit Talim Island or the prehistoric sites of Angono and Binangonan into a day trip. This guide is for travelers staying in Manila or Laguna who want to spend a day or half a day around the lake; prices and times that could not be confirmed are marked as "check locally." One more note on the environment: about Depending on how the area is counted, about 13 million people are known to live in the lake basin and surrounding cities, and household sewage, industrial waste, and pesticides and fertilizer flow into it along the rivers. Algae blooms that deplete oxygen have caused fish kills, and the lake is managed by the Laguna Lake Development Authority (LLDA, founded in 1966). Please visit with this reality in mind, leave no trash and respect local fishers and vendors.

Talim is the largest island in the lake and is governed by Binangonan (17 barangays) and Cardona (7 barangays) in Rizal, with a population of about 40,000 (2020). From the summit of Mount Tagapo, the highest point (locally called "Susong Dalaga"), you can see the Metro Manila skyline (Makati, Ortigas and others) far to the northwest on a clear day, and bamboo furniture and lake fishing are the island people's main livelihoods. There are few places to stay or eat on the island, so plan a day trip and bring drinking water.

blocks.title: The volcanic terrain of the Laguna Caldera

children.text: At the southern end of Talim Island is a crater landform about
3km

across, and maars (shallow pits left by volcanic explosions) have also been identified around Mayondon Hill in Los Baños and Tadlac Lake. Once you know the lake itself is a giant caldera, the same lakeside scenery looks different.

The western sky is open from almost anywhere on the shore, so the sunset is the easiest sight to enjoy. The De La Paz Esplanade in Biñan, the lakeside in Calamba and the pier area of Binangonan are often mentioned. After dark, fishing boat lights mix with the silhouettes of fish pens.

The lake is a major source of freshwater fish in the Philippines, and farmed species such as tilapia are common. At morning markets such as the Binangonan Public Market you can see freshly caught fish and local produce. This is where fishers work, so ask permission before taking photos.

blocks.title: Prehistoric rock carvings of Angono and Binangonan

children.text: Angono is known to have prehistoric rock carvings (petroglyphs), and they are easy to combine with a visit to the arts town of Angono in the same area. The protected site may not be open without a guide, so ask the local tourism office before you go.

The lake has Calamba Island (entirely occupied by the Wonder Island resort), Cielito Lindo Island off Cardona (privately owned), Bonga and Pihan islands, and Bay Island off the town of Bay, as far as is known (Calamba, Cielito Lindo and Bonga are consistent across sources; Pihan and Bay Island rest on a single Wikipedia source). Bay Island is tied to an old crocodile-deity legend, which makes it a good story. All are privately owned or may have restricted access, so check locally whether a visit is possible.

The road along Manila East Road through Angono, Binangonan, Cardona, Morong, Pililla and Tanay lets you see the lake scenery and old church towns together. Morong has a Spanish-era church whose facade and belltower form one connected landmark, and Pililla has a wind farm.
Drive from central Manila along Manila East Road to Angono. In heavy traffic the trip alone can take
1–2 hours
Browse the galleries and museums in the arts town of Angono.
Move to the lakeshore near Binangonan and look at the fish pens and the pier.
Watch the sunset from a good viewpoint on the shore and have dinner.
Head back to Manila, avoiding rush-hour traffic.
This course does not include a boat ride. If you want to see the glow from the water, find a boat at a local pier, but check the safety equipment and the fare first.
Leave Manila for the Binangonan pier (or the Cardona pier).
Cross to Talim Island by boat. The route and travel time vary with the weather and the water level.
Walk through the village and see the bamboo workshops and fishing scenes.
Have lunch at a local eatery or shop. Eateries may be few, so bring snacks and water.
If your strength and the weather allow, climb to the viewpoint on Mount Tagapo.
Before heading back to the mainland, check the last boat time locally.
Talim Island has simple facilities, so a day trip is easier than staying overnight.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) or central Manila, Angono and Binangonan are about
1–2 hours
by car. Manila East Road starts in Ortigas and runs through Cainta, Taytay, Angono and Binangonan to Cardona.
From the south (Laguna), use the roads through the cities on the lake's southern side, such as Calamba, Los Baños and Santa Rosa.
Traffic is heavy, so avoid weekday rush hours.

Jeepneys run along Manila East Road from places such as EDSA Crossing and Starmall, and many people transfer in Angono to a Binangonan jeepney. Guides also mention minibuses to Pililla from SM Masinag in Antipolo.
For Jala-jala you often have to transfer in Tanay or Pililla. Check routes and fares locally.
Boats to Talim Island leave from the Binangonan pier and the Cardona pier. Cardona is known as the smaller port.
No recent confirmed fares or schedules were found, so check directly on site. Service can be delayed when the lake rises or when water hyacinth is thick.
Check the condition of the pier and whether life jackets are provided.

The dry season in the Philippines is generally December to May. For walking around the lake and watching sunsets, the dry season with less rain is the most comfortable, and December to February is relatively cool and good for strolling through villages.

In the rainy season (June–November), typhoons and heavy rain can raise the lake and cause floods. Lakeside villages were also hit hard after Typhoon Ondoy (Ketsana) in 2009. If you go in the rainy season, check weather forecasts and local government announcements first.

Few resorts stand around the lake, so most travelers stay in Manila (Makati, Ortigas) or in Calamba, Los Baños or Santa Rosa in Laguna and visit the lake as a day trip. There are resorts on the lake, such as Wonder Island on Calamba Island, but check before booking, since operation and rates change over time. Talim Island is known to have almost no accommodation, so a day trip is recommended.

The signature food is freshwater fish from the lake. Grilled or fried tilapia and duck dishes near the lake (the area also has a duck industry) are often mentioned. Towns along Manila East Road have plenty of restaurants, and they thin out toward the outskirts, so bring water and snacks for outlying trips such as Talim Island. Eat street food only where you can see for yourself that it is hygienic.
It is best not to swim in the lake. The water is murky, there is almost no beach, and many fishing boats and fish pens make it unsafe.
Watch the sunset from a shore with an open western view, and arrange your ride back before dark.
Talim Island may lack a hospital and a market, so bring basic medicine, water and snacks.
When boarding a boat, check that life jackets are available, and postpone the trip if the weather is bad.
Ask permission before photographing fish pens and fishers at work.
Manila East Road is heavily congested, so travel outside weekday rush hours.
Bring insect repellent, an umbrella and a hat. Guides advise caution around mosquitoes (dengue) in this area.
Carry plenty of cash. ATMs are rare in small villages.
The lake has pollution and flood risks and is not a lake for swimming. In the rainy and typhoon seasons, check boat service and road conditions first.
Do not drink or wash with lake water. Water pollution has been a long-running problem.
When the lake rises in the rainy season, villages can flood and boats can stop.
Guides mention occasional petty theft on some stretches of Manila East Road, so keep valuables close.
Watch out for dogs, snakes and mosquitoes, and wear long pants for walks through grass or hikes.

Tanay Old Town and San Ildefonso Church
This waterfall lies upstream on the river that supplies about 35 percent of the lake's inflow, and
Pagsanjan Falls
is famous for its gorge boat rides.
Mount Makiling & Los Baños
on the south side of the lake has hot springs and forest, and the legend of the Makiling goddess is said to be linked to the story of the goddess of the lake.
In Calamba on the southwest side of the lake is the
Rizal Shrine Calamba
, which can be combined with a lakeside trip.
